parts.prompt:
Why must pressure be considered when comparing a water sample’s boiling point with 100 °C?
A. Pure water boils independently of pressure
B. Impurities alone change the boiling temperature
C. Pressure can change the boiling temperature
D. Reduced pressure demonstrates increased dissolved impurity
parts.canonical_answer:
C. Pressure can change the boiling temperature. Boiling occurs when vapour pressure matches the external pressure.
Distractor explanations: A: Even pure water has a pressure-dependent boiling point. B: Pressure as well as impurities can change boiling temperature. D: A pressure change is not evidence of dissolved impurity.
marking_guidance: Correct option C (1). C. Pressure can change the boiling temperature. Boiling occurs when vapour pressure matches the external pressure. Distractor explanations: A: Even pure water has a pressure-dependent boiling point. B: Pressure as well as impurities can change boiling temperature. D: A pressure change is not evidence of dissolved impurity. No mark for more than one selected option.

parts.prompt: Explain the conclusions from equal water portions needing 8.0 cm³ soap before boiling, 3.0 cm³ after boiling, and 1.0 cm³ after boiling followed by washing-soda treatment and filtration. The soft-water control needs 1.0 cm³; soap concentration and endpoint are constant.

parts.content_target: Investigate water hardness or purification with controlled volumes and evidence-based conclusions. Plan an investigation with predictions, suitable apparatus and techniques.
parts.credit_requirement: Plan hardness comparison: equal measured water volumes (1), fixed soap concentration (1), add soap in measured increments (1), standardise shaking (1), use persistent-lather endpoint (1), compare soap volumes to infer hardness (1).
parts.prompt: Plan a comparison of hardness for two water samples using soap solution. Include quantities, controlled procedure, a persistent-lather endpoint and how to interpret the data.
parts.canonical_answer: Measure equal 50.0 cm³ water portions into matching tubes. Add the same concentration of soap solution from a burette in measured increments, recording initial and final readings. Stopper and shake each for the same time and intensity after each addition, then observe whether lather remains for 30 s. Repeat trials and compare the soap volumes required. A larger volume indicates greater hardness because more soap reacts with dissolved calcium/magnesium before lasting lather forms. Keep water temperature, tube geometry and the lather criterion constant.
marking_guidance: Equal measured water volumes (1).
Same soap concentration (1).
Measured soap increments with volume record (1).
Standardised shaking (1).
Consistent persistent-lather endpoint, e.g. 30 s (1).
Compare soap volumes to infer hardness (1). Accept repetitions and sensible controls as supporting detail, not extra marks.
